title: What are the risks of overriding `equals()` but NOT `hashCode()`, and what happens in hash-based collections if only one is overridden or neither is?
shortTitle: What happens if you override equals() but not hashCode()?

s1_definition.profdef: Overriding equals without hashCode violates the equals-hashCode contract, because two objects that are now logically equal still return the identity-based hashCode inherited from Object, which is almost always different, so they are routed to different buckets in hash-based collections. The concrete risks are failed lookups where a HashMap.get with an equal key returns null, duplicate entries in a HashSet that should have rejected a logical duplicate, and generally unreliable containsKey and remove behavior. If neither method is overridden, equality falls back to reference identity and the collection works only when you use the exact same object reference, not a logically equal one.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, equals is the careful check that two account documents are the same, and hashCode is the drawer number used to file them. If you upgrade the sameness check but forget to also fix the drawer rule, two identical documents get filed in different drawers. Later you ask for the document by its details, the clerk computes a drawer from the old identity rule, opens the wrong drawer, finds nothing, and tells you the account does not exist, even though an identical document is sitting in another drawer. The paperwork is right, but the filing system fails.
s1_definition.oneliner: Overriding equals but not hashCode sends equal objects to different buckets, so HashMap lookups return null and HashSet stores duplicates; override both or neither works only by reference identity.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Overriding equals without hashCode violates the equals-hashCode contract, because two objects that are now logically equal still return the identity-based hashCode inherited from Object, which is almost always different, so they are routed to different buckets in hash-based collections. The concrete risks are failed lookups where a HashMap.get with an equal key returns null, duplicate entries in a HashSet that should have rejected a logical duplicate, and generally unreliable containsKey and remove behavior. If neither method is overridden, equality falls back to reference identity and the collection works only when you use the exact same object reference, not a logically equal one.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, equals is the careful check that two account documents are the same, and hashCode is the drawer number used to file them. If you upgrade the sameness check but forget to also fix the drawer rule, two identical documents get filed in different drawers. Later you ask for the document by its details, the clerk computes a drawer from the old identity rule, opens the wrong drawer, finds nothing, and tells you the account does not exist, even though an identical document is sitting in another drawer. The paperwork is right, but the filing system fails.

**One line to remember:** Overriding equals but not hashCode sends equal objects to different buckets, so HashMap lookups return null and HashSet stores duplicates; override both or neither works only by reference identity.

sections.s2_technical:
The inherited Object.hashCode is effectively based on object identity, so two distinct instances almost always have different hashCodes. The inherited Object.equals is also identity-based, so by default two distinct instances are never equal. When you override only equals, you change the sameness rule but leave the bucket rule tied to identity, and the two rules now disagree.

The failure in a HashMap is concrete. Storing uses the key's hashCode to choose a bucket. Looking up with an equal but different instance computes a different hashCode, selects a different bucket, and never reaches the stored entry, so get returns null, containsKey returns false, and remove does nothing:

```java
Map<Account, String> tier = new HashMap<>();
tier.put(new Account("SAV2001"), "PREMIUM");
tier.get(new Account("SAV2001"));       // null  (different bucket)
tier.containsKey(new Account("SAV2001"));// false
```

The failure in a HashSet is duplicates. A HashSet uses hashCode to find the candidate bucket and then equals to reject duplicates within it. If equal objects land in different buckets, the set never even compares them, so it stores both as if they were distinct, and the set that promised uniqueness now holds two logically equal elements:

```java
Set<Account> seen = new HashSet<>();
seen.add(new Account("SAV2001"));
seen.add(new Account("SAV2001"));
seen.size();  // 2  — duplicate NOT detected
```

If neither method is overridden, both equality and bucketing are identity-based and consistent with each other, so the collection behaves correctly, but only for the exact same reference. Two separately constructed accounts for SAV2001 are treated as different, which is fine only if that is genuinely what you want.

A senior point is that this bug is silent and intermittent-looking. It does not throw; it just loses data, so it often surfaces as a mysterious cache miss or a duplicate record in production. Another senior point is the fix is non-negotiable: whenever you override equals, you override hashCode from the same fields, and the reverse too, so the sameness rule and the bucket rule stay aligned. A final senior point is to prefer immutable keys and to generate both methods together with your IDE or a library to avoid hand-written drift.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A premium-tier map keyed by account returned null on lookup because the account class overrode equals but not hashCode. This is exactly the failed-lookup risk.

Problem 2 — A set meant to deduplicate accounts stored the same account twice for the same reason. This is exactly the duplicate-entry risk.

Problem 3 — After fixing the class to override both, the map lookup and the set deduplication both worked. This is exactly the resolution.

The code defines a `HalfAccount` with only equals overridden and a `FullAccount` with both overridden, and a `OnlyEqualsDemo` main class that shows the null lookup, the duplicate set, and then the correct behavior.

│   └── main/java/com/bank/core/
│       ├── HalfAccount.java        (equals only — risky)
│       ├── FullAccount.java         (equals + hashCode — correct)

# Compile
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/core/*.java

sections.s5_journey:
The inputs are a HalfAccount map and set and a FullAccount map and set, each used with separately constructed accounts for SAV2001.

Step 1: The HalfAccount map stores PREMIUM under a HalfAccount for SAV2001, placing it in a bucket chosen by the inherited identity hashCode.

Step 2: A lookup with a different HalfAccount for SAV2001 computes a different identity hashCode, selects a different bucket, finds nothing, and returns null, demonstrating the failed lookup.

Step 3: The HalfAccount set adds two separately constructed SAV2001 accounts. They land in different buckets, so equals is never consulted between them, and both are stored, giving a size of two, demonstrating the duplicate.

Step 4: The FullAccount map stores PREMIUM, this time bucketed by the account id, so a lookup with an equal FullAccount computes the same bucket, equals confirms, and PREMIUM is returned.

Step 5: The FullAccount set adds two equal accounts, which share a bucket, equals detects the duplicate, and the second add is rejected, giving a size of one, demonstrating correct deduplication.

```
Oct 30, 2026 ... WARNING: HalfAccount map lookup (expected null) → null
Oct 30, 2026 ... WARNING: HalfAccount set size (expected 2, duplicate!) → 2
Oct 30, 2026 ... INFO: FullAccount map lookup → PREMIUM
Oct 30, 2026 ... INFO: FullAccount set size (expected 1) → 1
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  HalfAccount (equals only)
    put(SAV2001) → bucket by identity(objA)
    get(SAV2001 twin) → bucket by identity(objB) ≠ A → null
    add x2 → different buckets → equals never runs → size 2 (duplicate)

  FullAccount (equals + hashCode)
    put(SAV2001) → bucket by hash(id)
    get(SAV2001 twin) → same bucket → equals → PREMIUM
    add x2 → same bucket → equals detects dup → size 1
```
sections.s5c_hld:

  ═══ HLD — Deduplication & Cache Correctness ═══

  ┌────────┐  REST  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ Client │───────→│ Dedup Service     │
  └────────┘        └───────┬──────────┘
                            │ Set<Account> / Map<Account,Tier>

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Half vs Full Override Risk ═══

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: equality and bucketing derive from one field, aligned│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────────┐
  │       HalfAccount          │   │        FullAccount         │
  │  + equals(Object)          │   │  + equals(Object)          │
  │  (identity hashCode)       │   │  + hashCode() = hash(id)   │
  └───────────────────────────┘   └───────────────────────────┘
     RISK: null lookups, dups          CORRECT behavior

  Behavior matrix (in sentences):
    equals only  → different buckets → failed lookups, duplicates
    hashCode only→ same bucket but identity equals → treated distinct
    neither      → identity for both → works only for same reference
    both         → aligned → correct lookups and dedup

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. tier.get(HalfAccount twin) → null
  2. half.size() → 2 (duplicate)
  3. tier2.get(FullAccount twin) → PREMIUM
  4. full.size() → 1
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The risk of overriding equals but not hashCode is that I break the equals-hashCode contract, because two objects that are now logically equal still return the identity-based hashCode inherited from Object, which is almost always different. In hash-based collections that means equal objects are routed to different buckets, and the collection quietly misbehaves.

Concretely, in a HashMap the store uses the key's hashCode to pick a bucket, and a lookup with an equal but separately constructed key computes a different hashCode, selects a different bucket, and never reaches the stored entry, so get returns null, containsKey returns false, and remove does nothing. In a HashSet the set uses hashCode to find the candidate bucket and then equals to reject duplicates, so if equal objects land in different buckets the set never compares them and stores both, and a container that promised uniqueness now holds a logical duplicate. I have seen exactly this surface in production as a mysterious cache miss and as duplicate records.

If neither method is overridden, both equality and bucketing fall back to identity and are at least consistent with each other, so the collection works, but only when I use the very same object reference, not a logically equal one. That is acceptable only when identity really is the intended notion of equality, which for value objects like an account it usually is not.

The fix is non-negotiable and symmetric: whenever I override equals I override hashCode from the same fields, and whenever I override hashCode I make equals consistent with it, so the sameness rule and the bucket rule always agree. I prefer immutable keys so those fields never change while the object is in a collection, and I generate both methods together with the IDE or a library so they cannot drift apart. So my complete answer is that overriding equals alone causes failed lookups and duplicate entries because equal objects scatter across buckets, and the professional rule is to always override both from the same stable fields.

---

keyPoints: Two equal objects may have different hash codes
HashMap/HashSet puts them in different buckets — lookup fails
Object appears lost: set.contains(equalObject) returns false
Always override both together — IDE can auto-generate them
